title: XL-SafetyBench: A Country-Grounded Cross-Cultural Benchmark for LLM Safety and Cultural Sensitivity
claim: One unified multi-stage construction pipeline, combining LLM generation, automated validation and native-speaker review, yields two complementary benchmarks.
layout: 2 stacked horizontal pipelines, left-to-right, country list with world map at left
description: The figure has a left column with a world map of blue pins and ten country flags with names: France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Spain, Türkiye, UAE and United States. Two wide stacked panels sit to its right. The top panel has a red border and is titled A. Jailbreak Benchmark. It contains pink boxes with numbered stages: harm categories, subcategory generation, base query generation and attack prompt generation. The last stage is an iterative attacker and judge loop. The flow ends in a red database icon labeled 450 attack prompts per country. The bottom panel has a green border and is titled B. Cultural Benchmark. Its green boxes cover cultural categories, sensitivity discovery and scenario generation. The flow ends in a green database icon labeled 100 scenario prompts per country. Chevron arrows link the stages. Robot, globe and people icons mark the LLM, web search and native-speaker validation steps. Red and green color-coding separates the two benchmarks.
caption: The XL-SafetyBench Construction Pipeline. A unified framework producing two complementary benchmarks. (A) Jailbreak Benchmark: generates country-grounded adversarial prompts via LLM-assisted discovery, base query generation, and an iterative attacker-judge red-teaming loop (450 prompts/country). (B) Cultural Benchmark: discovers country-specific sensitivities and embeds them as incidental details within tricky yet natural surface tasks (100 scenarios/country). Both combine LLM generation with automated validation gates and dual native-speaker validation.
abstract: Current LLM safety benchmarks are predominantly English-centric and often rely on translation, failing to capture country-specific harms. Moreover, they rarely evaluate a model's ability to detect culturally embedded sensitivities as distinct from universal harms. We introduce XL-SafetyBench, a suite of 5,500 test cases across 10 country-language pairs, comprising a Jailbreak Benchmark of country-grounded adversarial prompts and a Cultural Benchmark where local sensitivities are embedded within innocuous requests. Each item is constructed via a multi-stage pipeline that combines LLM-assisted discovery, automated validation gates, and dual independent native-speaker annotators per country. We report Attack Success Rate (ASR) alongside Neutral-Safe Rate (NSR) to separate principled refusal from non-engagement, and introduce the Cultural Sensitivity Rate (CSR) for recognizing embedded sensitivities. Evaluating 10 frontier and 27 local LLMs reveals two key findings. First, strong jailbreak robustness does not always come with strong cultural awareness, showing why the two should be evaluated separately. Second, local models exhibit a strong ASR-NSR trade-off (r = -0.81), suggesting that low attack success in several local models reflects non-engagement rather than safe refusal. XL-SafetyBench enables more nuanced, cross-cultural safety evaluation in the multilingual era.
